entries.3da3682518c66c2feddf15a4cb687434709685e6: <div sID="gen19622" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Dan.12" sID="Dan.12"/> <div eID="gen19622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19623" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19624" type="x-p"/> After the prediction of the troubles of the Jews under Antiochus, prefiguring the troubles of the Christian church under the anti-christian power, we have here, I. Comforts, and very precious ones, prescribed as cordials for the support of God's people in those times of trouble; and they are such as may indifferently serve both for those former times of trouble under Antiochus and those latter which were prefigured by them, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. A conference between Christ and an angel concerning the time of the continuance of these events, designed for Daniel's satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.5-Dan.12.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. III. Daniel's enquiry for his own satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.8">ver. 8</reference>. And the answer he received to that enquiry, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.9-Dan.12.12">ver. 9-12</reference>.
entries.d6f6c14f53d796b4a014840b1d7f2f9ad0b4fcc6: <div eID="gen19624" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19623" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Promised Appearance of Michael; The Prophecy Sealed Up. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 534.)</title> <div sID="gen19625" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people: and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation <hi type="italic">even</hi> to that same time: and at that time thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book. <hi type="super">2</hi> And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame <hi type="italic">and</hi> everlasting contempt. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever. <hi type="super">4</hi> But thou, O Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the time of the end: many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased. <div eID="gen19625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19626" type="x-p"/> It is usual with the prophets, when they foretel the grievances of the church, to furnish it at the same time with proper antidotes, a remedy for every malady. And no relief is so sovereign, of such general application, so easily accommodated to every case, and of such powerful efficacy, as those that are fetched from Christ and the future state; thence the comforts here are fetched. <div eID="gen19626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19627" type="x-p"/> I. Jesus Christ shall appear his church's patron and protector: <hi type="italic">At that time,</hi> when the persecution is at the hottest, <hi type="italic">Michael shall stand up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">v. 1</reference>. The angel had told Daniel what a firm friend Michael was to the church, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">ch. x. 21</reference>. He all along showed this friendship in the upper world; the angels knew it; but now <hi type="italic">Michael shall stand</hi> up in his providence, and work deliverance for the Jews, <hi type="italic">when he sees that their power is gone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">Deut. xxxii. 3</reference>. 6. Christ is <hi type="italic">that great prince,</hi> for he is the <hi type="italic">prince of the kings of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Rev. i. 5</reference>. And, if he stand up for his church, who can be against it? But this is not all: <hi type="italic">At that time</hi> (that is, soon after) Michael shall stand up for the working out of our eternal salvation; the Son of God shall be incarnate, shall be <hi type="italic">manifested to destroy the works of the devil.</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">stood for the children of our people</hi> when he was made sin and a curse for them, stood in their stead as a sacrifice, bore the cure for them, to bear it from them. He stands for them in the intercession he ever lives to make within the veil, stands up for them, and stands their friend. And after the destruction of antichrist, of whom Antiochus was a type, Christ shall <hi type="italic">stand at the latter day upon the earth,</hi> shall appear for the complete redemption of all his. <div eID="gen19627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19628" type="x-p"/> II. When Christ appears he will recompense tribulation to those that trouble his people. There shall <hi type="italic">be a time of trouble,</hi> threatening to all, but ruining to all the implacable enemies of God's kingdom among men, such <hi type="italic">trouble as never was since there was a nation.</hi> This is applicable. 1. To the destruction of Jerusalem, which Christ calls (perhaps with an eye to this prediction) such a <hi type="italic">great tribulation as was not since the beginning of the world to this time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.21">Matt. xxiv. 21</reference>. This the angel had spoken much of (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26-Dan.9.27">ch. ix. 26, 27</reference>); and it happened about the same time that Christ set up the gospel-kingdom in the world, that Michael our prince <hi type="italic">stands up.</hi> Or, 2. To the judgment of the great day, that day that shall <hi type="italic">burn as an oven,</hi> and consume the proud and all that do wickedly; that will be such a <hi type="italic">day of trouble</hi> as never was to all those whom Michael our prince stands against. <div eID="gen19628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19629" type="x-p"/> III. He will work salvation for his people: "<hi type="italic">At that time thy people shall be delivered,</hi> delivered from the mischief and ruin designed them by Antiochus, even all those that were marked for preservation, that were <hi type="italic">written among the living,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.4.3">Isa. iv. 3</reference>. When Christ comes into the world he will save his spiritual Israel from sin and hell, and will, at his second coming, complete their salvation, even the salvation of as many as were given him, as many as have <hi type="italic">their names in the book of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.20.15">Rev. xx. 15</reference>. They were written there before the world, and will be <hi type="italic">found written</hi> there at the end of the world, when the books shall be opened. <div eID="gen19629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19630" type="x-p"/> IV. There shall be a distinguishing resurrection of those that <hi type="italic">sleep in the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. When God works deliverance for his people from persecution it is a kind of resurrection; so the Jews' release out of Babylon was represented in vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.28">Ezek. xxxvii.</reference>) and so the deliverance of the Jews from Antiochus, and other restorations of the church to outward prosperity; they were as <hi type="italic">life from the dead. Many of those</hi> who had long slept in the dust of obscurity and calamity shall then awake, some to that life, and honour, and comfort which will be lasting, everlasting; but to others, who, when they return to their prosperity, will return to their iniquity, it will be a resurrection to shame and contempt, for the <hi type="italic">prosperity of fools</hi> will but expose them and destroy them. 2. When, upon the appearing of Michael our prince, his gospel is preached, many of those who <hi type="italic">sleep in the dust,</hi> both Jews and Gentiles, shall be awakened by it to take upon them a profession of religion, and shall rise out of their heathenism or Judaism; but, since there will be always a mixture of hypocrites with true saints, it is but some of those who are <hi type="italic">raised to life</hi> to whom the gospel is a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life,</hi> but others will be raised by it <hi type="italic">to shame and contempt,</hi> to whom the gospel of Christ will be a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death,</hi> and Christ himself set for their fall. The net of the gospel encloses both good and bad. But, 3. It must be meant of the general resurrection at the last day: <hi type="italic">The multitude of those that sleep in the dust shall awake,</hi> that is, all, which shall be a great many. Or, <hi type="italic">Of those that sleep in the dust</hi> many shall arise to life and many to shame. The Jews themselves understand this of the resurrection of the dead at the end of time; and Christ seems to have an eye to it when he speaks of the <hi type="italic">resurrection of life</hi> and the <hi type="italic">resurrection of damnation</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.29">John v. 29</reference>); and upon this the Jews are said by St. Paul to expect a <hi type="italic">resurrection of the dead both of the just and of the unjust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.24.15">Acts xxiv. 15</reference>. And nothing could come in more seasonably here, for, under Antiochus's persecution, some basely betrayed their religion, others bravely adhered to it. Now it would be a trouble to them that, when the storm was over, they could neither reward the one nor punish the other; this therefore would be a satisfaction to them, that they would both be recompensed according to their works in the resurrection. And the apostle, speaking of the pious Jews that suffered martyrdom under Antiochus, tells us that though they were tortured yet they <hi type="italic">accepted not deliverance,</hi> because they <hi type="italic">hoped to obtain this better resurrection,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">Heb. xi. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen19630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19631" type="x-p"/> V. There shall be a glorious reward conferred on those who, in the day of trouble and distress, being themselves <hi type="italic">wise,</hi> did <hi type="italic">instruct many.</hi> Such were taken particular notice of in the prophecy of the persecution (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.33">ch. xi. 33</reference>), that they should do eminent service, and yet should <hi type="italic">fall by the sword and by flame;</hi> now, if there were not another life after this, they would be <hi type="italic">of all men most miserable,</hi> and therefore we are here assured that they shall be recompensed <hi type="italic">in the resurrection of the just</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that are wise</hi> (that are <hi type="italic">teachers,</hi> so some read it, for teachers have need of wisdom, and those that have wisdom themselves should communicate it to others) <hi type="italic">shall shine as the brightness of the firmament,</hi> shall shine in glory, heavenly glory, the glory of the upper world; and those that by the wisdom they have, and the instructions they give, are instrumental <hi type="italic">to turn</hi> any, especially to <hi type="italic">turn many to righteousness,</hi> shall shine <hi type="italic">as the stars for ever and ever.</hi> Note, 1. There is a glory reserved for all the saints in the future state, for all that are wise, wise for their souls and eternity. A man's wisdom now <hi type="italic">makes his face to shine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Eccles. viii. 1</reference>), but much more will it do so in that state where its power shall be perfected and its services rewarded. 2. The more good any do in this world, especially to the souls of men, the greater will be their glory and reward in the other world. Those that turn <hi type="italic">men to righteousness,</hi> that <hi type="italic">turn sinners from the errors of their ways</hi> and help to <hi type="italic">save their souls from death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">Jam. v. 20</reference>), will share in the glory of those they have helped to heaven, which will be a great addition to their own glory. 3. Ministers of Christ, who have obtained mercy of him to be faithful and successful, and so are made <hi type="italic">burning and shining lights</hi> in this world, shall shine very brightly in the other world, shall shine <hi type="italic">as the stars.</hi> Christ is <hi type="italic">the sun,</hi> the fountain, of the lights both of grace and glory; ministers, as stars, shine in both, with a light derived from him, and a diminutive light in comparison of him; yet to those that are <hi type="italic">earthen vessels</hi> it will be a glory infinitely transcending their deserts. They shall <hi type="italic">shine as the stars</hi> of different magnitudes, some in less, others in greater lustre; but, whereas the day is coming when the stars shall fall from heaven as leaves in autumn, these stars shall <hi type="italic">shine for ever and ever,</hi> shall never set, never be eclipsed. <div eID="gen19631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19632" type="x-p"/> VI. That this prophecy of those times, though sealed up now, would be of great use to those that should live then, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">v. 4</reference>. Daniel must now <hi type="italic">shut up the words and seal the book</hi> because the <hi type="italic">time would be long</hi> ere these things would be accomplished: and it was some comfort that the Jewish nation, though, in the infancy of their return from Babylon, while they were few and weak, they met with obstructions in their work, were not persecuted for their religion till a long time after, when they had grown to some strength and maturity. He must <hi type="italic">seal the book</hi> because it would not be <hi type="italic">understood,</hi> and therefore would not be regarded, till the things contained in it were accomplished; but he must keep it safely, as a treasure of great value, laid up for the ages to come, to whom it would be of great service; for <hi type="italic">many shall then run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.</hi> Then this hidden treasure shall be opened, and many shall search into it, and dig for the knowledge of it, as for silver. They shall <hi type="italic">run to and fro,</hi> to enquire out copies of it, shall collate them, and see that they be true and authentic. They shall read it over and over, shall meditate upon it, and run it over in their minds; <hi type="italic">discurrent—they shall discourse</hi> of it, and talk it over among themselves, and compare notes about it, if by any means they may <hi type="italic">sift out</hi> the meaning of it; and thus <hi type="italic">knowledge shall be increased.</hi> By consulting this prophecy on this occasion they shall be led to <hi type="italic">search</hi> other <hi type="italic">scriptures,</hi> which shall contribute much to their advancement in useful knowledge; for <hi type="italic">then shall we know if we follow on to know the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Hos. vi. 3</reference>. Those that would have their knowledge increased must take pains, must not sit still in slothfulness and bare wishes but <hi type="italic">run to and fro,</hi> must make use of all the means of knowledge and improve all opportunities of getting their mistakes rectified, their doubts resolved, and their acquaintance with the things of God improved, to know more and to know better what they do know. And let us here see reason to hope that, 1. Those things of God which are now dark and obscure will hereafter be made clear, and easy to be understood. <hi type="italic">Truth is the daughter of time.</hi> Scripture prophecies will be expounded by the accomplishment of them; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they are given, and for that explication they are reserved. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they are <hi type="italic">told us before,</hi> that, <hi type="italic">when they do come to pass,</hi> we may believe. 2. Those things of God which are despised and neglected, and thrown by as useless, shall be brought into reputation, shall be found to be of great service, and be brought into request; for divine revelation, however slighted for a time, shall be <hi type="italic">magnified and made honourable,</hi> and, above all, in the <hi type="italic">judgment of the great day,</hi> when the books shall be opened, and that book among the rest.
entries.2b5997229dea43ef59c6d09692d2276a94d5d6c9: <div eID="gen19632" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Daniel's Solicitude to Know the Times; Period of Prophecy; Daniel Comforted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  534.)</title> <div sID="gen19633" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Then I Daniel looked, and, behold, there stood other two, the one on this side of the bank of the river, and the other on that side of the bank of the river. <hi type="super">6</hi> And <hi type="italic">one</hi> said to the man clothed in linen, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the waters of the river, How long <hi type="italic">shall it be to</hi> the end of these wonders? <hi type="super">7</hi> And I heard the man clothed in linen, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand unto heaven, and sware by him that liveth for ever that <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> for a time, times, and a half; and when he shall have accomplished to scatter the power of the holy people, all these <hi type="italic">things</hi> shall be finished. <hi type="super">8</hi> And I heard, but I understood not: then said I, O my Lord, what <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the end of these <hi type="italic">things?</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said, Go thy way, Daniel: for the words <hi type="italic">are</hi> closed up and sealed till the time of the end. <hi type="super">10</hi> Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried; but the wicked shall do wickedly: and none of the wicked shall understand; but the wise shall understand. <hi type="super">11</hi> And from the time <hi type="italic">that</hi> the daily <hi type="italic">sacrifice</hi> shall be taken away, and the abomination that maketh desolate set up, <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> a thousand two hundred and ninety days. <hi type="super">12</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that waiteth, and cometh to the thousand three hundred and five and thirty days. <hi type="super">13</hi> But go thou thy way till the end <hi type="italic">be:</hi> for thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days. <div eID="gen19633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19634" type="x-p"/> Daniel had been made to foresee the amazing revolutions of states and kingdoms, as far as the Israel of God was concerned in them; in them he foresaw troublous times to the church, suffering trying times, the prospect of which much affected him and filled him with concern. Now there were two questions proper to be asked upon this head:—<hi type="italic">When</hi> shall the <hi type="italic">end be?</hi> And, <hi type="italic">What</hi> shall the <hi type="italic">end be?</hi> These two questions are asked and answered here, in the close of the book; and though the comforts prescribed in the <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.4">foregoing verses</reference>, one would think, were satisfactory enough, yet, for more abundant satisfaction, this is added. <div eID="gen19634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19635" type="x-p"/> I. The question, <hi type="italic">When shall the end be?</hi> is asked by an angel, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.5-Dan.12.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Concerning this we may observe, <div eID="gen19635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19636" type="x-p"/> 1. Who it was that asked the question. Daniel had had a vision of Christ in his glory, the <hi type="italic">man clothed in linen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">ch. x. 5</reference>. But his discourse had been with the angel Gabriel, and now he <hi type="italic">looks,</hi> and <hi type="italic">behold other two</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.5">v. 5</reference>), two angels that he had not seen before, <hi type="italic">one upon the bank of the river on one side and the other on the other side,</hi> that, the river being between them, they might not whisper to one another, but what they said might be heard. Christ stood <hi type="italic">on the waters of the river,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">between the banks of Ulai;</hi> it was therefore proper that the angels his attendants should stand on either bank, that they might be ready to go, one one way and the other the other way, as he should order them. These angels appeared, (1.) To adorn the vision, and make it the more illustrious; and to add to the glory of the Son of man, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>. Daniel had not seen them before, though it is probable that they were there; but now, when they began to speak, he looked up, and saw them. Note, The further we look into the things of God, and the more we converse with them, the more we shall see of those things, and still new discoveries will be made to us; those that know much, if they improve it, shall know more. (2.) To confirm the discovery, that <hi type="italic">out of the mouth of two or three witnesses the word might be established.</hi> Three angels appeared to Abraham. (3.) To inform themselves, to hear and ask questions; for the mysteries of God's kingdom are things which the <hi type="italic">angels desire to look into</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1 Pet. i. 12</reference>) and they are <hi type="italic">known to the church,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Eph. iii. 10</reference>. Now one of these two angels said, <hi type="italic">When shall the end be?</hi> Perhaps they both asked, first one and then the other, but Daniel heard only one. <div eID="gen19636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19637" type="x-p"/> 2. To whom this question was put, to the <hi type="italic">man clothed in linen,</hi> of whom we read before (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">ch. x. 5</reference>), to Christ our great high priest, <hi type="italic">who was upon the waters of the river,</hi> and whose spokesman, or interpreter, the angel Gabriel had all this while been. This river was Hiddekel (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.4">ch. x. 4</reference>), the same with Tigris, the place whereabout many of the events prophesied of would happen; there therefore is the scene laid. Hiddekel was mentioned as one of the rivers that watered the garden of Eden (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.14">Gen. ii. 14</reference>); fitly therefore does Christ stand upon that river, for by him the trees in the paradise of God are watered. <hi type="italic">Waters</hi> signify <hi type="italic">people,</hi> and so his standing upon the waters denotes his dominion over all; he <hi type="italic">sits upon the flood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Ps. xxix. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">he treads upon the waters of the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.8">Job ix. 8</reference>. And Christ, to show that this was he, in the days of his flesh <hi type="italic">walked upon the waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.25">Matt. xiv. 25</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">above the waters of the river</hi> (so some read it); he appeared in the air over the river. <div eID="gen19637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19638" type="x-p"/> 3. What the question was: <hi type="italic">How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?</hi> Daniel would not ask the question, because he would not pry into what was hidden, nor seem inquisitive concerning the times and the seasons, which the Father has <hi type="italic">put in his own power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Acts i. 7</reference>. But, that he might have the satisfaction of the answer, the angel put the question in his hearing. Our Lord Jesus sometimes answered the questions which his disciples were afraid or ashamed to ask, <reference osisRef="John.16.19">John xvi. 19</reference>. The angel asked as one concerned, <hi type="italic">How long shall it be?</hi> What is the time prefixed in the divine counsels for the <hi type="italic">end of these wonders,</hi> these suffering trying times, that are to pass over the people of God? Note, (1.) The troubles of the church are the <hi type="italic">wonder</hi> of angels. They are astonished that God will suffer his church to be thus afflicted, and are anxious to know what good he will do his church by its afflictions. (2.) Good angels know no more of things to come than God is pleased to discover to them, much less do evil angels. (3.) The holy angels in heaven are concerned for the church on earth, and lay to heart its afflictions; how much more then should we, who are more immediately related to it, and have so much of our peace in its peace? <div eID="gen19638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19639" type="x-p"/> 4. What answer was returned to it by him who is indeed the <hi type="italic">numberer of secrets,</hi> and knows things to come. <div eID="gen19639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19640" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a more general account given of the continuance of these troubles to the angel that made the enquiry (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">v. 7</reference>), that they shall continue <hi type="italic">for a time, times, and a half,</hi> that is, a year, two years, and half a year, as was before intimated (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">ch. vii. 25</reference>), but the one half of a prophetical week. Some understand it indefinitely, a certain time for an uncertain; it shall be <hi type="italic">for a time</hi> (a considerable time), for <hi type="italic">times</hi> (a longer time yet, double what it was thought at first that it would be), and yet indeed it shall be but <hi type="italic">half a time,</hi> or a part of a time; when it is over it shall seem not half so much as was feared. But it is rather to be taken for a certain time; we meet with it in the Revelation, under the title sometimes of three days and a half, put for three years and a half, sometimes forty-two months, sometimes 1260 days. Now this determination of the time is here [1.] Confirmed by an oath. The man <hi type="italic">clothed in linen</hi> lifted up both his hands <hi type="italic">to heaven, and swore by him that lives for ever and ever</hi> that it should be so. Thus the <hi type="italic">mighty angel</hi> whom St. John saw is brought in, with a plain reference to this vision, standing with his <hi type="italic">right foot on the sea</hi> and <hi type="italic">his left foot on the earth,</hi> and with his hand lifted up to heaven, swearing <hi type="italic">that there shall be no longer delay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.10.5-Rev.10.6">Rev. x. 5, 6</reference>. This Mighty One that Daniel saw stood with <hi type="italic">both feet</hi> on the water, and swore with <hi type="italic">both hands</hi> lifted up. Note, An oath is of use for confirmation; God only is to be sworn by, for he is the proper Judge to whom we are to appeal; and lifting up the hand is a very proper and significant sign to be used in a solemn oath. [2.] It is illustrated with a reason. God will suffer him to prevail <hi type="italic">till he shall have accomplished to scatter the power of the holy people.</hi> God will suffer him to do his worst, and run his utmost length, and then <hi type="italic">all these things shall be finished.</hi> Note, God's time to succour and relieve his people is when their affairs are brought to the last extremity; <hi type="italic">in the mount of the Lord it shall be seen</hi> that Isaac is saved just when he lies ready to be sacrificed. Now the event answered the prediction; Josephus says expressly, in his book of the <hi type="italic">Wars of the Jews,</hi> that Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, surprised Jerusalem by force, <hi type="italic">and held it three years and six months,</hi> and was then <hi type="italic">cast out of the country</hi> by the Asmoneans or Maccabees. Christ's public ministry continued <hi type="italic">three years and a half,</hi> during which time he endured the contradiction of sinners against himself, and lived in poverty and disgrace; and then when his power seemed to be quite scattered at his death, and his enemies triumphed over him, he obtained the most glorious victory and said, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> <div eID="gen19640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19641" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is something added more particularly concerning the time of the continuance of those troubles, in what is said to Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.11-Dan.12.12">v. 11, 12</reference>, where we have, [1.] The event fixed from which the time of the trouble is to be dated, from the <hi type="italic">taking away of the daily sacrifice</hi> by Antiochus, and the <hi type="italic">setting up</hi> of the image of Jupiter upon the altar, which was the <hi type="italic">abomination of desolation.</hi> They must reckon their troubles to begin indeed when they were deprived of the benefit of public ordinances; that was to them the <hi type="italic">beginning of sorrows;</hi> that was what they laid most to heart. [2.] The continuance of their trouble; it shall last 1290 days, <hi type="italic">three years</hi> and <hi type="italic">seven months,</hi> or (as some reckon) <hi type="italic">three years, six months,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fifteen days;</hi> and then, it is probable, the daily sacrifice was restored, and the abomination of desolation taken away, in remembrance of which the <hi type="italic">feast of dedication</hi> was observed even to our Saviour's time, <reference osisRef="John.10.22">John x. 22</reference>. Though it does not appear by the history that it was exactly so long to a day, yet it appears that the beginning of the trouble was in the 145th year of the Seleucidæ, and the end of it in the 148th year; and either the restoring of the sacrifice, and the taking away of the image, were just so many days after, or some other previous event that was remarkable, which is not recorded. There are many particular times fixed in the scripture-prophecies, which it does not appear by any history, sacred or profane, that the event answered, and yet no doubt it did punctually; as <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa. xvi. 14</reference>. [3.] The completing of their deliverance, or at least a further advance towards it, which is here set forty-five days after the former, and, some think, points at the death of Antiochus, 1335 days after his profaning the temple. <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that waits and comes</hi> to that time. It is said (<reference osisRef="1Macc.9.28">1 Mac. ix. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Macc.10.1">x. 1</reference>) that the Maccabees, under a divine conduct, <hi type="italic">recovered the temple and the city.</hi> Many good interpreters make these to be prophetical days (that is, so many years), and date them from the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans; but what events they then fall upon they are not agreed. Others date them from the corruption of the gospel-worship by the antichrist, whose reign is confined in the Apocalypse to 1260 days (that is, years), at the end of which he shall begin to fall; but thirty years after he shall be quite fallen, at the end of 1290 days; and whoever lives forty years longer, to 1335 days, will see glorious times indeed. Whether it looks so far forward or no I cannot tell; but this, however, we may learn, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That there is a time fixed for the termination of the church's troubles, and the bringing about of her deliverance, and that this time will be punctually observed to a day. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That this time must be waited for with faith and patience. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That, when it comes, it will abundantly recompense us for our long expectations of it. <hi type="italic">Blessed is he</hi> who, having waited long, comes to it at last, for he will then have reason to say, <hi type="italic">Lo, this is our God, and we have waited for him.</hi> <div eID="gen19641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19642" type="x-p"/> II. The question, <hi type="italic">What shall the end be?</hi> is asked by Daniel, and an answer given to it. Observe, <div eID="gen19642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19643" type="x-p"/> 1. Why Daniel asked this question; it was because, though he <hi type="italic">heard what was said</hi> to the angel, yet he did not <hi type="italic">understand</hi> it, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.8">v. 8</reference>. Daniel was a very intelligent man, and had been conversant in visions and prophecies, and yet here he was puzzled; he did not understand the meaning of the <hi type="italic">time, times, and the part of a time,</hi> at least not so clearly and with so much certainty as he wished. Note, The best men are often much at a loss in their enquiries concerning divine things, and meet with that which they do not <hi type="italic">understand.</hi> But the better they are the more sensible they are of their own weaknesses and ignorance, and the more ready to acknowledge them. <div eID="gen19643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19644" type="x-p"/> 2. What the question was: <hi type="italic">O my Lord! What shall be the end of these things?</hi> He directs his enquiry not to the angel that talked with him, but immediately to Christ, for to whom else should we go with our enquiries? "What shall be the final issue of these events? What do they tend to? What will then end in?" Note, When we take a view of the affairs of this world, and of the church of God in it, we cannot but think, What will be the end of these things? We see things move as if they would end in the utter ruin of God's kingdom among men. When we observe the prevalence of vice and impiety, the decay of religion, the sufferings of the righteous, and the triumphs of the ungodly over them, we may well ask, <hi type="italic">O my Lord! what will be the end of these things?</hi> But this may satisfy us in general, that all will end well at last. Great is the truth, and will prevail at long-run. All opposing rule, principality, and power, will be put down, and holiness and love will triumph, and be in honour, to eternity. The end, this end, will come. <div eID="gen19644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19645" type="x-p"/> 3. What answer is returned to this question. Besides what refers to the time (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.11-Dan.12.12">v. 11, 12</reference>), of which before, here are some general instructions given to Daniel, with which he is dismissed from further attendance. <div eID="gen19645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19646" type="x-p"/> (1.) He must content himself with the discoveries that had been made to him, and not enquire any further: "<hi type="italic">Go thy way, Daniel;</hi> let it suffice thee that thou has been admitted thus far to the foresight of things to come, but stop here. <hi type="italic">Go thy way</hi> about the king's business again, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.27">ch. viii. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">Go thy way,</hi> and record what thou hast seen and heard, for the benefit of posterity, and covet not to see and hear more at present." Note, Communion with God is not our continual feast in this world; we sometimes are taken to be witnesses of Christ's glory, and we say, <hi type="italic">It is good to be here;</hi> but we must go down from the mount, and have there no continuing city. Those that know much <hi type="italic">know but in part,</hi> and still see there is a great deal that they are kept in the dark about, and are likely to be so till the veil is rent; hitherto their knowledge shall go, but no further. "<hi type="italic">Go thy way, Daniel,</hi> satisfied with what thou hast." <div eID="gen19646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19647" type="x-p"/> (2.) He must not expect that what had been said to him would be fully understood till it was accomplished: <hi type="italic">The words are closed up and sealed,</hi> are involved in perplexities, and are likely to be so, <hi type="italic">till the time of the end,</hi> till the end of these things; nay, till the end of all things. Daniel was ordered to <hi type="italic">seal the book to the time of the end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">v. 4</reference>. The Jews used to say, <hi type="italic">When Elias comes he will tell us all things.</hi> "They are <hi type="italic">closed up and sealed,</hi> that is, the discovery designed to be made by them is now fully settled and completed; nothing is to be added to it nor taken from it, for it is <hi type="italic">closed up</hi> and <hi type="italic">sealed;</hi> ask not therefore after more." <hi type="italic">Nescire velle quæ magister maximus docere non vult erudita inscitia est—He has learned much who is willing to be ignorant of those things which the great teacher does not choose to impart.</hi> <div eID="gen19647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19648" type="x-p"/> (3.) He must count upon no other than that, as long as the world stands, there will still be in it such a mixture as now we see there is of good and bad, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.10">v. 10</reference>. We long to see all wheat and no tares in God's field, all corn and no chaff in God's floor; but it will not be till the time of ingathering, till the winnowing day, comes; both must <hi type="italic">grow together until the harvest.</hi> As it has been, so it is, and will be, <hi type="italic">The wicked shall do wickedly,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the wise shall understand.</hi> In this, as in other things, St. John's Revelation closes as Daniel did. <reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Rev. xxii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">He that is filthy, let him be filthy still; and he that is holy, let him be holy still.</hi> [1.] There is no remedy but that wicked people <hi type="italic">will do wickedly;</hi> and such people there are and will be in the world to the end of time. <hi type="italic">So said the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceeds from the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">1 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>); and the observation of the moderns says the same. Bad men will do bad things; and a <hi type="italic">corrupt tree</hi> will <hi type="italic">never bring forth good fruit.</hi> Do men <hi type="italic">gather grapes of thorns,</hi> or bring forth good things from an evil treasure in the heart? No; wicked practices are the natural products of wicked principles and dispositions. <hi type="italic">Marvel not at the matter</hi> then, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>. We are told, before, that the <hi type="italic">wicked will do wickedly;</hi> we can expect no better from them: but, which is worse, <hi type="italic">none of the wicked shall understand.</hi> This is either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A part of their sin. They <hi type="italic">will not understand;</hi> they shut their eyes against the light, and none so blind as those that will not see. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they are <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> because they <hi type="italic">will not understand.</hi> If they did but rightly know the truths of God, they would readily obey the laws of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>. Wilful sin is the effect of wilful ignorance; they <hi type="italic">will not understand</hi> because <hi type="italic">they are wicked;</hi> they <hi type="italic">hate the light,</hi> and come not to the light, <hi type="italic">because their deeds are evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.19">John iii. 19</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a part of their punishment; they will do wickedly, and therefore God has given them up to <hi type="italic">blindness of mind,</hi> and has said concerning them, <hi type="italic">They shall not understand,</hi> nor be <hi type="italic">converted and healed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.14-Matt.13.15">Matt. xiii. 14, 15</reference>. God will not <hi type="italic">give them eyes to see,</hi> because they will do wickedly, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.4">Deut. xxix. 4</reference>. [2.] Yet, bad as the world is, God will secure to himself a remnant of good people in it; still there shall be some, there shall be many, to whom the providences and ordinances of God shall be <hi type="italic">a savour of life unto life,</hi> while to others they are <hi type="italic">a savour of death unto death. First,</hi> the providences of God shall do them good: <hi type="italic">Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried,</hi> by their troubles (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.11.35">ch. xi. 35</reference>), by the same troubles which will but stir up the corruptions of the wicked and make them do more wickedly. Note, The afflictions of good people are designed for their trial; but by these trials they are <hi type="italic">purified</hi> and <hi type="italic">made white,</hi> their corruptions are purged out, their graces are brightened, and made both more vigorous and more conspicuous, and are <hi type="italic">found to praise, and honour, and glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 7</reference>. To those who are themselves sanctified and good every event is sanctified, and works for good, and helps to make them better. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The word of God shall do them good. When the <hi type="italic">wicked understand not,</hi> but stumble at the word, the <hi type="italic">wise shall understand.</hi> Those who are wise in practice shall understand doctrine; those who are influenced and governed by the divine law and love shall be illuminated with a divine light. For if any man will <hi type="italic">do his will</hi> he shall <hi type="italic">know the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser.</hi> <div eID="gen19648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19649" type="x-p"/> (4.) He must comfort himself with the pleasing prospect of his own happiness in death, in judgment, and to eternity, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.13">v. 13</reference>. Daniel was now very old, and had been long engaged both in an intimate acquaintance with heaven and in a great deal of public business on this earth. And now he must think of bidding farewell to this present state: <hi type="italic">Go thou thy way till the end be.</hi> [1.] It is good for us all to think much of going away from this world; we are still going, and must be gone shortly, gone the way of all the earth. That must be our way; but this is our comfort, We shall not go till God calls for us to another world, and till he has done with us in this world, till he says, "<hi type="italic">Go thou thy way;</hi> thou hast finished thy testimony, done thy work, and accomplished as a hireling thy day, therefore now, <hi type="italic">Go thy way,</hi> and leave it to others to take thy room." [2.] When a good man goes his way from this world he enters into rest: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt rest</hi> from all thy present toils and agitations, and shalt not see the evils that are coming on the next generation." Never can a child of God say more pertinently than in his dying moments, <hi type="italic">Return unto thy rest, O my soul!</hi> [3.] Time and days will have an end; not only our time and days will end very shortly, but all times and days will have an end at length; yet a little while, and time shall be no more, but all its revolutions will be numbered and finished. [4.] Our rest in the grave will be but <hi type="italic">till the end of the days;</hi> and then the peaceful rest will be happily disturbed by a joyful resurrection. Job foresaw this when he said of the dead, <hi type="italic">Till the heavens be no more,</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep,</hi> implying that then they shall, <reference osisRef="Job.14.12">Job xiv. 12</reference>. [5.] We must every one of us <hi type="italic">stand in our lot at the end of the days.</hi> In the judgment of the great day we must have our allotment according to what we were, and what we did, in the body, either, <hi type="italic">Come, you blessed</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Go, you cursed;</hi> and we must <hi type="italic">stand for ever in that lot.</hi> It was a comfort to Daniel, it is a comfort to all the saints, that, whatever their lot is in the days of time, they shall have a happy lot in <hi type="italic">the end of the days,</hi> shall have their <hi type="italic">lot among the chosen.</hi> And it ought to be the great care and concern of every one of us to secure a happy lot at last in the <hi type="italic">end of the days,</hi> and they we may well be content with our present lot, welcome the will of God. [6.] A believing hope and prospect of a blessed lot in the heavenly Canaan, at the end of the days, will be an effectual support to us when we are going our way out of this world, and will furnish us with living comforts in dying moments.  <chapter eID="Dan.12"/> <div eID="gen19649" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen19310" osisID="Dan" type="book"/>

entries.68d6bbcc8b63d16f6fa4d19a00d132fdcd4029f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12228"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.13">Da 12:1-13</reference>. Conclusion of the Vision (Tenth through Twelfth Chapters) AND Epilogue to the Book.</title> <div sID="gen22241" type="x-p"/> Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Da 12:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.13">13</reference>; as <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">Da 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">7</reference> refer to <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>, that is, to the time of Antichrist, so the subsequent <reference osisRef="Dan.12.8-Dan.12.12">Da 12:8-12</reference> treat of the time of Antiochus (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.12.11">Da 12:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">Da 11:31</reference>), thus putting together in one summary view the two great periods of distress. The political resurrection of the Jews under the Maccabees is the starting-point of transition to the literal resurrection about to follow the destruction of Antichrist by Christ's coming in glory. The language passes here from the nearer to the more remote event, to which alone it is fully applicable.<div eID="gen22241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12228"/><hi type="bold">1. at that time--</hi>typically, towards the close of Antiochus' reign; antitypically, the time when Antichrist is to be destroyed at Christ's coming.<div eID="gen22242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Michael--</hi>the guardian angel of Israel ("thy people"), (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>). The transactions on earth affecting God's people have their correspondences in heaven, in the conflict between good and bad angels; so at the last great contest on earth which shall decide the ascendency of Christianity (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.7-Rev.12.10">Re 12:7-10</reference>). An archangel, not the Lord Jesus; for he is distinguished from "the Lord" in Jude 9.<div eID="gen22243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall be--</hi>rather, "it shall be."<div eID="gen22244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time of trouble, such as never was--</hi>partially applicable to the time of Antiochus, who was the first subverter of the Jews' religion, and persecutor of its professors, which no other world power had done. Fully applicable to the last times of Antichrist, and his persecutions of Israel restored to Palestine. Satan will be allowed to exercise an unhindered, unparalleled energy (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jr 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.21">Mt 24:21</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Dan.8.24">Da 8:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">11:36</reference>).<div eID="gen22245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy people shall be delivered--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>). The same deliverance of Israel as in <reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>, "the third part ... brought through the fire ... refined as silver." The remnant in Israel spared, as not having joined in the Antichristian blasphemy (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.9">Re 14:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">10</reference>); not to be confounded with those who have confessed Christ before His coming, "the remnant according to the election of grace" (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>), part of the Church of the first-born who will share His millennial reign in glorified bodies; the spared remnant (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Is 10:21</reference>) will only know the Lord Jesus when they see Him, and when the spirit of grace and supplication is poured out on them [Tregelles].<div eID="gen22246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">written in the book--</hi>namely, of God's secret purpose, as destined for deliverance (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.28">69:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.15">Re 20:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">21:27</reference>). Metaphor from a muster-roll of citizens (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.5">Ne 7:5</reference>). <div eID="gen22247" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c540a9086afc8df2c3915d07e77a1df07969fec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12229"/><div sID="gen22248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12229"/><hi type="bold">2. many ... that sleep--</hi>"many from among the sleepers ... these shall be unto everlasting life; but those (the rest of the sleepers who do not awake at this time) shall be unto shame" [Tregelles]. Not the general resurrection, but that of those who share in the first resurrection; the rest of the dead being not to rise till the end of the thousand years (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">Re 20:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">5, 6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">1Co 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>). Israel's national resurrection, and the first resurrection of the elect Church, are similarly connected with the Lord's coming forth out of His place to punish the earth in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Is 26:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.6">27:6</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6-Isa.25.9">Is 25:6-9</reference>. The Jewish commentators support Tregelles. Auberlen thinks the sole purpose for which the resurrection is introduced in this verse is an incitement to faithful perseverance in the persecutions of Antiochus; and that there is no chronological connection between the time of trouble in <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference> and the resurrection in <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>; whence the phrase, "at that time," twice occurs in <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>, but no fixing of time in <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference> Maccabees 7:9, 14, 23, shows the fruit of this prophecy in animating the Maccabean mother and her sons to brave death, while confessing the resurrection in words like those here. Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">He 11:35</reference>. Newton's view that "many" means all, is not so probable; for <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">19</reference>, which he quotes, is not in point, since the Greek is "the many," that is, all, but there is no article in the Hebrew here. Here only in the Old Testament is "everlasting life" mentioned. <div eID="gen22248" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae58b8b764aeb6610998aeb6f686e4ffc9732ef3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12230"/><div sID="gen22249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12230"/><hi type="bold">3. wise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.11.30">Pr 11:30</reference>). Answering to "they that understand" (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.33">Da 11:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.35">35</reference>), the same Hebrew, Maskilim; Israelites who, though in Jerusalem when wickedness is coming to a head, are found intelligent witnesses against it. As then they appeared worn out with persecutions (typically, of Antiochus; antitypically, of Antichrist); so now in the resurrection they "shine as the brightness of the firmament." The design of past afflictions here appears "to make them white" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Mt 13:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen22249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn ... to righteousness--</hi>literally, "justify," that is, convert many to justification through Christ (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">Jas 5:20</reference>).<div eID="gen22250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stars--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.41">1Co 15:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.42">42</reference>). <div eID="gen22251" type="x-p"/>
entries.06d32c5374eda27ef144ac37d51390ef2cf4ccc7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12231"/><div sID="gen22252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12231"/><hi type="bold">4. shut up ... seal the book--</hi>John, on the contrary, is told (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.10">Re 22:10</reference>) not to seal his visions. Daniel's prophecy refers to a distant time, and is therefore obscure for the immediate future, whereas John's was to be speedily fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Re 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference>; 22:6). Israel, to whom Daniel prophesied after the captivity, with premature zeal sought after signs of the predicted period: Daniel's prophecy was designed to restrain this. The Gentile Church, on the contrary, for whom John wrote, needs to be impressed with the shortness of the period, as it is, owing to its Gentile origin, apt to conform to the world, and to forget the coming of the Lord (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.25.13">Mt 25:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.13.32-Mark.13.37">Mr 13:32-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2Pe 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Re 22:20</reference>).<div eID="gen22252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run to and fro--</hi>not referring to the modern rapidity of locomotion, as some think, nor to Christian missionaries going about to preach the Gospel to the world at large [Barnes], which the context scarcely admits; but, whereas now but few care for this prophecy of God, "at the time of the end," that is, near its fulfilment, "many shall run to and fro," that is, scrutinize it, running through every page. Compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.2">Ha 2:2</reference> [Calvin]: it is thereby that "the knowledge (namely, of God's purposes as revealed in prophecy) shall be increased." This is probably being now fulfilled. <div eID="gen22253" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffdc0b00c108df8ffa046371a05476ea2c177ad9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12232"/><div sID="gen22254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12232"/>5. A vision of two other angels, one on one side of the Hiddekel or Tigris, the other on the other side, implying that on all sides angels attend to execute God's commands. The angel addressing Daniel had been over the river "from above" (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">Da 12:6</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen22254" type="x-p"/>
entries.adf7ca6fc58c31a430ed2eb72514963b84721210: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12233"/><div sID="gen22255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12233"/><hi type="bold">6. one--</hi>namely, of the two (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.5">Da 12:5</reference>).<div eID="gen22255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man ... in linen--</hi>who had spoken up to this point. God impelled the angel to ask in order to waken us out of our torpor, seeing that the very "angels desire to look into" the things affecting man's redemption (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>), as setting forth the glory of their Lord and ours (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen22256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">How long ... to the end of these wonders--</hi>This question of the angel refers to the final dealings of God in general, Antichrist's overthrow, and the resurrection. Daniel's question (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.8">Da 12:8</reference>) refers to the more immediate future of his nation [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen22257" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc5e42be8ba7622dc608ac50a283c4b26d5e061e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12234"/><div sID="gen22258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12234"/><hi type="bold">7. held up ... right ... and ... left hand--</hi>Usually the right hand was held up in affirmation as an appeal to heaven to attest the truth (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.40">De 32:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.10.5">Re 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">6</reference>). Here both hands are lifted up for the fuller confirmation.<div eID="gen22258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time, times, and a half--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>). Newton, referring this prophecy to the Eastern apostasy, Mohammedanism, remarks that the same period of three and a half years, or 1260 prophetic days, is assigned to it as the Western apostasy of the little horn (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>); and so, says Prideaux, Mohammed began to forge his imposture, retiring to his cave, A.D. 606, the very year that Phocas made the grant to the bishop of Rome, whence he assumed the title, The Universal Pastor; Antichrist thus setting both his feet on Christendom together, the one in the East, and the other in the West. Three and a half is the time of the world power, in which the earthly kingdoms rule over the heavenly [Auberlen]. "Three and a half" represents the idea of spiritual trial; (besides this certain symbolical meaning, there is doubtless an accurate chronological meaning, which is as yet to us uncertain): it is half of "seven," the complete number, so a semi-perfect state, one of probation. The holy city is trodden by the Gentiles forty-two months (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.2">Re 11:2</reference>), so the exercise of the power of the beast (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.5">Re 13:5</reference>). The two witnesses preach in sackcloth 1260 days, and remained unburied three days and a half: so the woman in the wilderness: also the same for a "time, times, and a half" (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.3">Re 11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.11">9, 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.14">14</reference>). Forty-two connects the Church with Israel, whose haltings in the wilderness were forty-two (<reference osisRef="Num.33.1-Num.33.50">Nu 33:1-50</reference>). The famine and drought on Israel in Elijah's days were for "three years and six months" (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.25">Lu 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">Jas 5:17</reference>); there same period as Antiochus' persecution: so the ministry of the Man of Sorrows, which ceased in the midst of a week (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>) [Wordsworth, Apocalypse].<div eID="gen22259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scatter ... holy people--</hi>"accomplished" here answers to "the consummation" (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>), namely, the "pouring out" of the last dregs of the curse on the "desolated holy people." Israel's lowest humiliation (the utter "scattering of her power") is the precursor of her exaltation, as it leads her to seek her God and Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.39">Mt 23:39</reference>). <div eID="gen22260" type="x-p"/>
entries.30a17da44e81d09f269d4e3ef70133ff90ea2257: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12235"/><div sID="gen22261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12235"/><hi type="bold">8. understood not--</hi>Daniel "understood" the main features of the vision as to Antiochus (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.1">Da 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">14</reference>), but not as to the times. <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10-1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:10-12</reference> refers mainly to Daniel: for it is he who foretells "the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow"; it is he who prophesies "not unto himself, but unto us"; it is he who "searched what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ in him did signify." <div eID="gen22261" type="x-p"/>
entries.81c4d0deb14d01c24009218fe856350dd2e13307: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12236"/><div sID="gen22262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12236"/>9. Daniel's desire of knowing more is thus deferred "till the time of the end." John's Revelation in part reveals what here is veiled (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Da 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.26">Da 8:26</reference>). <div eID="gen22262" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2689e395c0e25eda27143992023412b060ba1ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12237"/><div sID="gen22263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12237"/>10. There is no need of a fuller explanation as to the time; for when the predictions so far given shall have come to pass, the godly shall be "purified" by the foretold trials and shall understand that the end is at hand; but the wicked shall not understand, and so shall rush on to their own ruin (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.33-Dan.11.35">Da 11:33-35</reference>) [Maurer]. The "end" is primarily, of Antiochus' persuasion; antitypically, the end of Antichrist's. It is the very clearness in the main which renders necessary the obscurity. The fulfilment of God's decree is not a mere arithmetical problem which the profane may understand by arithmetical calculations, but a holy enigma to stimulate to a faithful observance of God's ways, and to a diligent study of the history of God's people [Auberlen]. To this Christ refers (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Mt 24:15</reference>), "Whose readeth, let him understand." <div eID="gen22263" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe58b83df6fb18b59efeaf91cfef1f38cafceac3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12238"/><div sID="gen22264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12238"/><hi type="bold">11. from ... sacrifice ... taken way ... abomination--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">Da 11:31</reference>). As to this epoch, which probably is prophetically germinant and manifold; the profanation of the temple by Antiochus (in the month Ijar of the year 145 B.C., till the restoration of the worship by Judas Maccabeus on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month [Chisleu] of 148 B.C., according to the Seleucid era, 1290 days; forty-five days more elapsed before Antiochus' death in the month Shebat of 148 B.C., so ending the Jews' calamities [Maurer]); by pagan Rome, after Christ's death; by Mohammed; by Antichrist, the culmination of apostate Rome. The "abomination" must reach its climax (see Auberlen's translation, "summit," <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>), and the measure of iniquity be full, before Messiah comes.<div eID="gen22264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thousand two hundred and ninety days--</hi>a month beyond the "time, times, and a half" (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Da 12:7</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Dan.12.12">Da 12:12</reference>, forty-five days more are added, in all 1335 days. Tregelles thinks Jesus at His coming will deliver the Jews. An interval elapses, during which their consciences are awakened to repentance and faith in Him. A second interval elapses in which Israel's outcasts are gathered, and then the united blessing takes place. These stages are marked by the 1260, 1290, and 1335 days. Cumming thinks the 1260 years begin when Justinian in A. D. 533 subjected the Eastern churches to John II, bishop of Rome; ending in 1792, when the Code Napoleon was established and the Pope was dishonored. 1290 reach to 1822, about the time of the waning of the Turkish power, the successor to Greece in the empire of the East. Forty-five years more end in 1867, the end of "the times of the Gentiles." See <reference osisRef="Lev.26.24">Le 26:24</reference>, "seven times," that is, 7 X 360, or 2520 years: 652 B.C. is the date of Judah's captivity, beginning under Manasseh; 2520 from this date end in 1868, thus nearly harmonizing with the previous date, 1867. See on <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Da 8:14</reference>. The seventh millenary of the world [Clinton] begins in 1862. Seven years to 1869 (the date of the second advent) constitute the reign of the personal Antichrist; in the last three and a half, the period of final tribulation, Enoch (or else Moses) and Elijah, the two witnesses, prophesy in sackcloth. This theory is very dubious (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">Mt 24:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2">1Th 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>); still the event alone can tell whether the chronological coincidences of such theories are fortuitous, or solid data on which to fix the future times. Hales makes the periods 1260, 1290, 1335, begin with the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and end with the precursory dawn of the Reformation, the preaching of Wycliffe and Huss. <div eID="gen22265" type="x-p"/>
entries.007dc09571a71f11d5e54a706672fbf1781f5730: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12239"/><div sID="gen22266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12239"/><hi type="bold">13. rest--</hi>in the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.3.17">Job 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Is 57:2</reference>). He, like his people Israel, was to wait patiently and confidently for the blessing till God's time. He "received not the promise," but had to wait until the Christian elect saints should be brought in, at the first resurrection, that he and the older Old Testament saints "without us should not be made perfect" (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">He 11:40</reference>).<div eID="gen22266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand--</hi>implying justification unto life, as opposed to condemnation (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Psa 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen22267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy lot--</hi>image from the allotment of the earthly Canaan. <chapter eID="Dan.12"/><div eID="gen22268" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen21529" osisID="Dan" type="book"/>

entries.757e003ff0762935cfa312b788847bef8b485422: <div eID="gen33443" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33444" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33445" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33445" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33444" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33446" type="x-p"/> The proper conclusion to the great revolutions predicted in this and the following chapters is the general resurrection, of which the beginning of this chapter (to be literally understood) gives some intimation, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.3">Dan 12:1-3</reference>. Daniel is then commanded to shut up the words and to seal the book to the time of the end, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Dan 12:4</reference>; and is informed of the three grand symbolical periods of a time, times, and a half, twelve hundred and ninety days and thirteen hundred and thirty-five days, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4-Dan.12.12">Dan 12:4-12</reference>; at the end of the last of which Daniel shall rest and stand in his lot, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.13">Dan 12:13</reference>. It is generally thought by commentators that the termination of the last period is the epoch of the First resurrection. See <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Rev 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.5">Rev 20:5</reference>. <div eID="gen33446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33447" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33448" type="x-p"/> And at that time Michael shall stand up - Michael the archangel, as has already been observed, was ever reputed the guardian of the Jewish people. <div eID="gen33448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33449" type="x-p"/> Every one that shall be found written in the book - All that truly fear, love, and obey the Lord, On the phrase, "written in the book, the book of life," etc., see the passages in the margin, and the notes on those passages.
entries.90fa988a51508314ed3fa31389c9cb1204a949a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33450" type="x-p"/> Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth - This prophecy has been referred to the future restoration of the Jews. It will be also true of the state of mankind at the general judgment.
entries.aaeb3da2f83fc2991ee138d49545dd07110d4357: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33451" type="x-p"/> And they that be wise - Those who are thoroughly instructed in Christ's word and doctrine, shall shine - shall be eminently distinguished in the Christian Church by the holiness of their lives, and the purity of their creed. <div eID="gen33451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33452" type="x-p"/> And they that turn many to righteousness - They who, by preaching Christ crucified among their brethren, shall be the means of converting them to the Christian faith; shall be as the stars - bright luminaries in the Gospel kingdom of Jesus Christ. This also may be applied to the case of holy and useful men, particularly the faithful ministers of the Gospel, in the day of judgment. See <reference osisRef="Jam.5.20">Jam 5:20</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.41-1Cor.15.42">1Cor 15:41-42</reference> (note).
entries.91eaa75005c2f9f0ad35578b8525ebdbb85006c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33453" type="x-p"/> Shut up the words, and seal the book - When a prophet received a prediction concerning what was at a considerable distance of time, he shut his book, did not communicate his revelation for some time after. This Daniel was commanded to do, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.26">Dan 8:26</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Isa.29.10">Isa 29:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.11">Isa 29:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.10">Rev 22:10</reference>. Among the ancients, those were said to seal, who in the course of their reading stamped the places of which they were yet doubtful, in order to keep them in memory, that they might refer to then; again, as not yet fully understood. This custom Salmasius, in his book De modo Usurarum, p. 446, proves from Hesychius. <div eID="gen33453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33454" type="x-p"/> Many shall run to and fro - Many shall endeavour to search out the sense; and knowledge shall be increased by these means; though the meaning shall not be fully known till the events take place: Then the seal shall be broken, and the sense become plain. This seems to be the meaning of this verse, though another has been put on it, viz., "Many shall run to and fro preaching the Gospel of Christ, and therefore religious knowledge and true wisdom shall be increased." This is true in itself; but it is not the meaning of the prophet's words.
entries.90b913d9288e90045ff2444a65e47c7dc8e11fab: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33455" type="x-p"/> Behold there stood other two - Probably two angels. We know no more of them, unless they be the same as those called saints, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference> (note), which see. The river was most likely the Tigris.
entries.3f61e0f6ac8ac116e2cbd32e4f2163e21631b031: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33456" type="x-p"/> The man clothed in linen - Gabriel in a human form. Thus he is represented, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Dan 10:5</reference>.
entries.be49431f7bbf0c8125c79bd2b22e4ad5c8f11f4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33457" type="x-p"/> Which was upon the waters - By this description, he was standing on the water. This is very similar to the description of the angel, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.5">Rev 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">Rev 10:6</reference>, and in the seventh verse there seems to be a reference to this prophecy "a time, times, and a half." See the note on <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference> (note).
entries.bb6698e629699178b6e35a319133d072f6294ab5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33458" type="x-p"/> I heard, but I understand not - Could not comprehend what the time, times, and half time should refer to. These make three years and a half of prophetic times answering to one thousand two hundred and sixty years.
entries.68bcfab557ca4edff81bc67a466e79cec6e1ed08: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33459" type="x-p"/> The words are closed up - The prophecy shall not be understood, but in its accomplishment; and then the depth of the wisdom and providence of God will be clearly seen in these matters. See on Daniel 4 (note). We must wait "till the time of the end;" and this, it appears from the following calculations, will not arrive before the Twentieth Century. We here see the reason why these prophecies are at present so imperfectly understood. God has sealed them.
entries.cf28c42b49ad40821adbdb0dd25575c12b30ed26: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33460" type="x-p"/> Many shall be purified - During the interim, the great work of God's providence and grace shall be carried on in the salvation of men; who, in the midst of trials, temptations, and difficulties, shall be purified and made white - be fully saved from their sins. <div eID="gen33460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33461" type="x-p"/> None of the wicked shall understand - Because they are wicked, and will continue in their sins, the eyes of their understanding shall be closed, and their hearts hardened; so that they shall not see the light of the glorious Gospel. <div eID="gen33461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33462" type="x-p"/> But the wise - Those who open their hearts to God, that he may pour in his light, shall understand the things that make for their peace.
entries.93cb51782e0cfeb056e1a9b9a52b354ad310fa34: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33463" type="x-p"/> From the time that the daily sacrifice shall be taken away - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Dan.11.25-Dan.11.27">Dan 11:25-27</reference> (note). <div eID="gen33463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33464" type="x-p"/> The abomination that maketh desolate set up - I believe, with Bp. Newton, that this is a proverbial phrase; and may be applied to any thing substituted in the place of, or set up in opposition to, the ordinances of God, his worship, his truth, etc. Adrian's temple, built in the place of God's temple at Jerusalem, the church of St. Sophia turned into a Mohammedan mosque, etc., etc., may be termed abominations that make desolate. Perhaps Mohammedanism may be the abomination; which sprang up a.d. 612. If we reckon one thousand two hundred and ninety years, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.11">Dan 11:11</reference>, from that time, it will bring us down to a.d. 1902, when we might presume from this calculation, that the religion of the False Prophet will cease to prevail in the world; which from the present year, 1825, is distant only seventy-seven years.
entries.f89dac018394d9a3c58a61dcd690bd871b0f139a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33465" type="x-p"/> Blessed is he that waiteth - He who implicitly depends on God, expecting, as his truth cannot fail, that these predictions shall be accomplished in due time. <div eID="gen33465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33466" type="x-p"/> And cometh to the thousand three hundred and five and thirty days - This is seventy-five days more than what is included in the three years and a half, or the time, times, and a half in the seventh verse; and as we have met with so many instances of prophets days and years, this undoubtedly is another instance; and as a day stands for a year, this must mean a period of one thousand three hundred and thirty-five years, which period is to bring all these wonders to an end, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">Dan 12:6</reference>. But we are left totally in the dark relative to the time from which these one thousand three hundred and thirty-five years are to be reckoned. If, however, we reckon them from the above epoch, a.d. 612, when Mohammedanism arose, they lead us to a.d. 1947, when the fullness of the Gentiles shall be brought in; and thus a final closure of vision and prophecy be made, as then all the great events relative to the salvation of men shall have taken place. Wars and contentions will probably then cease over the whole world; Jews and Gentiles become one fold, under one Shepherd and Bishop of souls; and the triune God be properly worshipped and glorified, from generation to generation, over the face of the whole earth. But all these conjectures may be founded in darkness. We have not chronological data; and "the times and seasons God has reserved in his own power."
entries.9efc7e96abab404ac9b1342231364ec72cf0c747: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33467" type="x-p"/> But go thou thy way till the end be - Here is proper advice for every man. <div eID="gen33467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33468" type="x-p"/> 1. Thou hast a way - a walk in life, which God has assigned thee; walk in that way, it is thy way. <div eID="gen33468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33469" type="x-p"/> 2. There will be an end to thee of all earthly things. Death is at the door, and eternity is at hand; go on to the end - be faithful unto death. <div eID="gen33469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33470" type="x-p"/> 3. There is a rest provided for the people of God. Thou shalt rest; thy body, in the grave; thy soul, in the Divine favor here, and finally in paradise. <div eID="gen33470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33471" type="x-p"/> 4. As in the promised land there was a lot for each of God's people, so in heaven there is a lot for thee. Do not lose it, do not sell it, do not let thy enemy rob thee of it. Be determined to stand in thy own lot at the end of the days. See that thou keep the faith; die in the Lord Jesus, that thou mayest rise and reign with him to all eternity.
